items.title: UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements
items.summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is set to outline the proposals today, in a move which could prompt Israel to retaliate.
items.content:
The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.

Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.

The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.

One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different.

"It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."

But Labour MPs who have been briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement, according to a number of MPs present.

The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.

Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.

An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US - which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals - has not commented.

Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty - who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister - told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.

He said: "At the moment, we can sanction where there is evidence of it being linked to settler violence, but not, for example, in relation to a contractor working on the settlements. We need to expand our sanctions powers."

While ministers are said to recognise that banning a relatively small quantity of mostly agricultural products is a largely symbolic gesture, the government is expected to frame this announcement as a major reset in Britain's wider policy on Israel.

The expected announcement by the UK government comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.

Speaking in his first address to Parliament as foreign secretary last week, Miliband said those plans were "illegal under international law", and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's announcement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

Tuesday's expected intervention will come almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.

The government believes the prospect of a two-state solution is being jeopardised by the rapid expansion of settlements.

The proposal for an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital, to exist alongside Israel has received international backing over several decades.

It proposes an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital. It would exist alongside Israel.

Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.

The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.

Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

How Israel is expanding settlements in drive to reshape West Bank

'Israeli settlers laid siege to our home': Inside a Palestinian village under weekly attack

Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow

items.title: Trial over alleged murders of Australian surfer brothers starts in Mexico
items.summary: The bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend were found with gunshot wounds to their heads.
items.content:
Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.

The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California.

Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft.

The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult".

"We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC.

"Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away."

On the opening day, the accused - Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants.

Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial.

The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada.

Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns.

The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders.

Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader.

Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory.

Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player.

His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding.

items.title: I've factored the RSA keys of a Certificate Authority from the 90s
items.summary: Article URL: https://mcpherrin.ca/2026/09/07/rsa.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49604637 Points: 243 # Comments: 45
items.content:
I’ve been thinking about the security of RSA lately. RSA’s cryptography relies on the difficulty of factoring a large semiprime number, but what “large” means is an interesting question. The Web PKI deprecated 1024-bit RSA over a decade ago, and while I don’t know of anyone factoring a key of that size, it’s within the realm of possibility for a government or other organization with a large number of computers. Just a few days ago, someone factored the 862-bit RSA-260 key from the RSA factoring challenge. That’s the largest factorization I’m aware of. Today, the world uses RSA of at least 2048 bits, but even that will be deprecated soon with the risk of quantum computers in the future.

This led me to wonder: small RSA keys can be factored on even a modest desktop computer. And in the early days of the Web PKI, there were no standards, and no minimum requirements. Netscape shipped SSL support in 1994, and IE shortly afterwards. This was still the era of export restrictions on cryptography. Are there any keys small enough that I can factor? I don’t have any good reason to do that, but it seems like fun.

The spoiler is of course, yes, but first we need to find a key to crack.

Fortunately, root certificates were shipped with browser installers, and there are archives of both Internet Explorer and Netscape on archive.org. The archives aren’t comprehensive, but they should provide good coverage of old root CAs. I downloaded both collections and set Claude Code on extracting all the roots. I’ve hosted a Claude-generated webpage with all those old-timey, ancient roots . While I haven’t verified this LLM output is entirely trustworthy, it looks pretty plausible.

Using the filters on that site, we can find what small keys are trusted for SSL.

Aha! We have a target. Back in March 1999, Netscape 4.51 shipped a 512-bit RSA certificate authority trusted for SSL, and another for S/MIME. These two roots were both from the long-defunct Canadian certificate authority called E-Certify .

Later that year, the 512-bit RSA-155 was factored, so even in its era this was too weak and probably shouldn’t have shipped in the first place.

The E-Certify 512-bit roots were removed by Netscape in 2002. Unfortunately, Internet Explorer seems to have never shipped any 512-bit roots for SSL, so our fun will be limited to Netscape from a relatively small time frame.

Factoring the public keys in the root certificates will give me the two primes that I need to reconstruct the private key. I ran CADO-NFS on my Ryzen 9 5950X desktop; it took 32 hours to factor E-Certify RSA 512 Gold Server for SSL, and another 29 hours for E-Certify RSA 512 Gold Client for S/MIME. You can get the resulting private keys below.

Assuming you’re somehow running Netscape 4.51 with a clock set before E-Certify roots expired on 2003-10-16, you can use these private keys to issue certificates. This describes zero people on the planet… except for this VM I set up.

Verifying that the issued certificates would work in Netscape 4.51 was an adventure in itself, as there is zero overlap in TLS capability between Netscape 4.51 and any modern TLS stack. So it was back to Claude Code to make a custom old-timey TLS server in Go. This site is publicly hosted at e-certify.fly.dev , which you are welcome to try out with your own copy of Netscape, but it won’t load in any modern browser.

Or, if you’d like to host your own website using these old-timey keys, the keys and tools are all in the repo at https://github.com/mcpherrinm/ancientroots . Or do worse, like MitM the SSL of all those Netscape 4.51 users with their clocks set to 25 years ago…

As a bonus, Internet Explorer 3.02 shipped a code signing CA called OU=Test VeriSign Commercial Software Publisher CA. I’m not sure what that’s for, but it’s just as easily factored. There are a few other test-looking 512-bit RSA keys in the ancient roots repo, so you should try factoring some more of them, or seeing what they could be used for!

Steve Weis factored this one in about an hour using a GPU cluster.

items.title: Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
items.summary: In his resignation letter, Ruslan Kravchenko denied the allegations against him, saying he did not want his office "to be used as a tool in political confrontation".
items.content:
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.

It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.

In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".

Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.

According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".

The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.

Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.

He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.

Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.

In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.

Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.

Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.

Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.

Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering .

A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.

In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team.

"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said.

During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption.

Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine.

However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption.

"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC.

Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, sacked minister tells BBC

items.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
items.summary: The threat against one of Canada's largest companies comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours.
items.content:
President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank'."

The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to be imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) worth of US goods.

In a statement, Bombardier underscored that it employed thousands of American workers and said it valued its partnerships with American companies.

The BBC has reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney's office for comment.

It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.

The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.

It also operates sites in Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, DC and New Jersey.

About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

In a statement on Monday, Bombardier did not address Trump's threat directly, but said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs through the company's growing American footprint".

"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," its statement said. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country."

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.

The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.

It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.

In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".

She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.

On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."

"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.

items.title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff protest after female workers moved for religious visit
items.summary: An investigation will be launched into the incident, which left female employees "humiliated", a union representative says.
items.content:
The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.

A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.

Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move.

"During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident.

"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.

She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."

Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.

The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".

They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".

SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice.

"I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."

The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.

BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.

In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".

It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".

On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.

It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit.

"I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X.

"Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."

French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."

Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

items.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
items.summary: Tukaram Mundhe has gone viral after a series of aggressive inspections of restaurants to detect hygiene lapses.
items.content:
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.

One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.

At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.

Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.

"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.

The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.

Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.

But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.

Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.

But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.

The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.

Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five , external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.

And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.

By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.

Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.

"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".

Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.

The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.

However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.

Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.

His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered , external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.

The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".

The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?

Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.

For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.

"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.

He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."

The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.

Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.

But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.

"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.

The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.

For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.

"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

items.title: TALA Is Open-Source
items.summary: Article URL: https://d2lang.com/blog/tala-is-open-source/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49604150 Points: 170 # Comments: 12
items.content:
Following up on the announcement here , TALA (Terrastruct's AutoLayout Algorithm) is now open-source under the same license as D2 (MPL-2.0).

TALA is a novel autolayout algorithm designed with software architecture diagrams in mind. This means it's primarily an orthogonal layout engine, which more closely matches what you might find on whiteboards, rather than the DAG-based ones that grow in one direction. It blends ideas from different graph-drawing research papers (cited in source code) along with original techniques to achieve aesthetic diagrams. It considers multiple objectives of "aesthetic", including symmetry, median distance, flow, clustering of like nodes, and much more.

TALA comes bundled into D2 v0.9.0, so just install and specify with --layout=tala to try it out! Or head on over to https://play.d2lang.com , which runs 100% client-side. I especially look forward to the improvements that being open-source brings, and can't wait to see what improvements and ideas are submitted by the community.

Special thanks to Gavin Nishizawa for substantial broad contributions across TALA, and Júlio César Batista for his work on hierarchy algorithms and more. It was so fun getting to work on such interesting stuff with you guys.

items.title: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
items.summary: The head of chip designer Arm says modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer cannot be done now, but computers are "going to solve it".
items.content:
The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.

Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.

Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.

However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.

Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.

Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.

Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast : "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.

"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.

"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.

Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.

He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.

"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.

"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."

In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.

"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."

Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.

He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.

Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.

This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.

The CEO of chip design company Arm tells the BBC AI will help cure cancer, lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but says its rapid growth is being held up by a shortage of chips needed in data centres.

There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.

He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.

"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."

But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.

"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."

As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.

But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

OpenAI chief scientist warns no one is prepared for consequences of AI

items.title: Flight recorders recovered from Amazon cargo plane crash
items.summary: Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport.
items.content:
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.

Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway as it attempted to land shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.

The plane hit two vehicles - a cleaning van carrying seven people and a Toyota with three passengers.

NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".

Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.

The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.

It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla , coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.

"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well."

She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."

The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.

Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.

Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.

The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.

Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots (48km/h).

The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.

Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.

"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."

Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash . Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.

The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.

Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.

The company operating the aircraft, 21 Air, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.

Video shows damaged Amazon cargo plane after crash kills five

Investigators begin work on why cargo plane overran Miami runway

items.title: Il Canada pronto a far scattare i dazi sul 'Made in Usa'
items.summary: Entrano in vigore l'8 settembre, i più colpiti sono Michigan e Ohio
items.content:
Entrano in vigore l'8 settembre i dazi del Canada contro gli Stati Uniti, decisi dal premier Mark Carney in ritorsione alle tariffe americane in seguito alLE fallite trattative commerciali. I dazi canadesi colpiranno soprattutto gli esportatori americani in Michigan e in Ohio, dove i repubblicani sono in difficoltà in vista delle elezioni di metà mandato. L'entrata in vigore delle tariffe rischia di infiammare la guerra commerciale fra i due paesi vicini.

Donald Trump torna ad attaccare il Canada e chiude a Bombardier il mercato americano. "Basta vendere prodotti Bombardier negli Stati Unit! I loro prodotti non sono all'altezza. Oltre il 50% del loro fatturato proviene dagli Stati Uniti: vivono grazie ad acquirenti, aziende, aeroporti e servizi americani, mentre il Canada ostacola le nostre grandi banche e aziende americane", ha detto il presidente sul suo social Truth. "Se vogliono accedere al nostro mercato, devono produrre qui e smetterla di trattare l'America come un salvadanaio. Comprate prodotti americani, volate su aerei americani, gustatevi alcolici e bebande americani. L'America prima di tutto", ha messo in evidenza.

items.title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
items.summary: A headteacher in the occupied West Bank has installed new barbed wire fencing after three pupils were killed this year.
items.content:
On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank.

"We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

"I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.

Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot.

"When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."

He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.

The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.

Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.

Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.

Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.

In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".

With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.

The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection.

BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank

Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village

'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC

"I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades.

"We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."

But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.

Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.

Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.

Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared.

"They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."

We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.

Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that.

"At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."

Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.

A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children , external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."

And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".

Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.

At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.

Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder.

"In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."

The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before.

"You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said. "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."

Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said.

"No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"

The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting.

"We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."

Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk.

"Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."

UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.

This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.

All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.

The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.

items.title: Serie A: Frattesi guida la rimonta, a Udine la Lazio si regala la vetta
items.summary: Il centrocampista-goleador e Gudmundsson rispondono al vantaggio di Karlstrom
items.content:
UDINESE - Lazio 1-0 al 49'! Rete di Jesper Karlström . Sponda di Davis, il centrocampista con un colpo di biliardo mette la palla tra le gambe di Mandas.

Udinese-LAZIO 1-1 al 79'! Rete di Davide Frattesi. Zaccagni passa Vojvoda e crossa al centro, l'ex Inter é il primo ad arrivare sul pallone e segnare la sua terza rete stagionale.

Udinese-LAZIO 1-2 all'88'! Rete di Albert Gudmundsson. Doekhi con il pallone perfetto per l'islandese che bagna il suo esordio in maglia Lazio.

Vittoria e aggancio a Inter e Roma in testa alla classifica. E' una Lazio sfavillante quella che passa a Udine (2-1) con una rimonta tutta volontà e corsa. Adesso i biancocelesti attendono il Milan per un big match che può addirittura regalare il primato in solitaria, almeno per qualche ora, visto che le avversarie giocheranno soltanto lunedì prossimo. Un sogno a occhi aperti per i 2.500 tifosi che hanno raggiunto il Friuli per i propri beniamini.

Decisive le reti del solito Frattesi - una sorta di attaccante aggiunto - e di Gudmundsson: quando il mercato creativo e a saldo zero vale più di investimenti milionari. Runjaic esclude a sorpresa Kabasele, a vantaggio di Ebosse, con Solet spostato al centro della difesa. In avanti, a supporto di Davis, ci sono Gomez ed Ekkelenkamp. Gattuso sceglie il tridente con Isaksen, Pinamonti e capitan Zaccagni.

Lazio subito pericolosa: al 4' Tavares semina il panico a sinistra e mette al centro, ma Solet salva in corner su Pinamonti pronto al tap-in. Risponde l'Udinese al 12': Davis prima impegna Mandas in tuffo in diagonale, ma il portiere ospite si supera sulla ribattuta di Kamara respingendo di piede. Primo cambio al quarto d'ora, Piotrowski, appena ammonito, non ce la fa e Runjac propone il ventenne scozzese Miller.

Non ci sono pause e al 21' sono ancora i biancocelesti a mettere i brividi: Vojvoda sbaglia il retropassaggio ma Zaccagni, a tu per tu con Okoye, mette debolmente al centro permettendo al neo entro Miller di salvare in extremis prima dell'arrivo di Pinamonti. Non c'è pace per Runjaic: al 38' anche Solet si stira e deve entrare Kabasele. Vista la carenza di slot, Runjaic approfitta dell'intervallo per sostituire un impalpabile Gomez con Bayo, passando al 3-5-2 classico.

La mossa paga subito dividendo perché al 4' l'Udinese passa in vantaggio con un'azione da manuale: palla al centro per Davis che di tacco mette Karlstrom davanti a Mandas. La conclusione dello svedese passa tra le gambe del portiere in uscita disperata. E' la prima rete subita dalla squadra di Gattuso in questa Serie A. Il tecnico corre ai ripari e sostituisce la linea offensiva: fuori Isaksen e Pinamonti e dentro Noslin e Cancellieri.

Il pressing degli ospiti diventa asfissiante e al 17' Okoye respinge il colpo di testa da due passi di Zaccagni. Ospiti ancora a un passo dal pari al 28': dopo una volata di Frattesi la palla arriva a Cancellieri, ma Kamara si immola e salva sulla riga. Il gol è nell'aria e arriva due minuti dopo con la solita incursione di Frattesi che brucia sul tempo la difesa e insacca di punta sotto la traversa un perfetto cross di capitan Zaccagni.

Runjaic capisce l'antifona e rinforza gli ormeggi richiamando in panchina Davis e Abankwah avvicendati da Bertola e Zarraga. Gattuso sente l'odore del sangue e del sorpasso e propone Gudmundsson per Frattesi, alla terza rete in tre giornate. La Lazio spinge e Zaccagni al 42' colpisce un palo clamoroso con Okoye immobile. L'Udinese è alle corde e al 43' capitola: Vojvoda perde un pallone sanguinoso in uscita e Doekhi vede l'accorrente Gudmundsson che, da centro area, di testa, non perdona e porta a Roma i 3 punti e il primo posto in graduatoria.

items.title: Leaving VMware just got harder after Broadcom pulled VDDK downloads
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.virtualizationhowto.com/2026/09/leaving-vmware-just-got-harder-after-broadcom-pulled-vddk-downloads/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49602699 Points: 165 # Comments: 71
items.content:
Just when we thought that Broadcom wouldn’t be able to slow down customers moving off of vSphere to another platform. They may just now have done something that will have that net effect. This time it involves VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit, which we have always known as the VDDK. Broadcom has just killed the download of this library, and it will have far reaching consequences if this is a permanent move. Let’s see why this is a cause for alarm and why the VDDK is so important.

If you have never personally downloaded the VDDK you might assume this is some obscure VMware developer package that most just won’t ever need. And, you are right to some extent if you have no need to use the VDDK directly. However, what you might not realize is just how many tools that you probably ARE using that make use of it. Like what?

Well, here is the kicker. This library is central to many of the migration tools that are used to migrate from VMware to other platforms. It is used by tools like Microsoft Azure Migrate, Red Hat’s Migration Toolkit, Nutanix Move, VMware to KVM migration products, and other tools like virtv2v and nbdkit . So, for VMware customers who are trying to figure out what life after Broadcom looks like, this is yet another unexpected roadblock to leaving the platform.

The reason this suddenly matters is that Broadcom has removed the normal publicly accessible VDDK download pages , and affected customers are reporting that Broadcom support has told them VDDK is no longer available for general use or download. See the Reddit thread here: Broadcom VDDK links : r/sysadmin .

If you now navigate to the link of the VDDK download where it was previously, you will see the following 404 page:

Even stranger as it would seem, I have been unable to find a traditional Broadcom announcement explaining this change. So far, there has been no transition notice, deprecation announcement, or replacement tool or library announced.

Instead of this, many migration vendors and customers have seen in the last few day that links they have been pointed to are suddenly returning errors. This is much more interesting than an SDK just disappear. So, the net effect, no matter what Broadcom’s motivation might be is pretty hard for us to ignore at this point.

A VMware technology that is used to move and protect VMware workloads has now become harder for customers and migration vendors to get their hands on. For many customers who may be looking at their exit path from VMware, this feels like just another obstacle placed in the exit path from the platform.

The company ShapeBlue has documented the change as of August 25, 2026. They discovered that the VMware VDDK pages referenced in the VMware to KVM migration documentation were returning error. They then went on to test numerous VDDK URL paths that included version specific paths for VDDK 8 and 9. However, both versions are showing to be unavailable.

ShapeBlue documented the change on August 25, 2026, after discovering that the VMware VDDK pages referenced by its VMware-to-KVM migration workflow were returning errors. ShapeBlue tested numerous VDDK paths, including version-specific locations for VDDK 8 and 9, and reported that all of them were unavailable. You can read ShapeBlue’s detailed announcement on the VDDK removal here: Broadcom Removes VDDK Pages Without Explanation: What You Need to Know .

They made the observation that Broadcom has not published a public announcement where they explain the reasoning behind this being removed, withdrawn, or deprecated. Very interesting.

One of the strongest pieces of evidence we have so far that this is an intentional withdrawal of the bits for the VDDK comes from Broadcom customers who have opened up support cases. You will find the discussion on the Reddit thread interesting. A customer posted the response they received directly from Broadcom Customer Care.

The customer on the Reddit thread reported that Broadcom told them the VDDK was “ no longer available for use or download “. They also pointed the customer back to backup and recovery products from authorized Broadcom Technology Alliance Partners. Again, read this for yourself on the Reddit thread here .

There is another recent Reddit discussion on the official VMware Reddit thread’s subreddit on the topic. Users there are reporting the same thing. One admin said they opened a ticket with Broadcom and were told by support the VDDK had been intentionally removed and was no longer available through the previous method.

Another discussion in the VMware subreddit contains users reporting essentially the same thing. One administrator said they opened a ticket with Broadcom and support confirmed VDDK had been intentionally removed and was no longer available through the previous method. Read the VMware community discussion in this sub Reddit here. The post was recently removed by VMware moderators but you can still see the comments on the thread here: [ Removed by moderator ] : r/vmware .

So, I think the writing is on the wall here that it is difficult for us to just chock this up to some sort of website glitch where the VDDK has disappeared.

However, we may have even stronger evidence from an equally large company as Broadcom, Microsoft. Microsoft has now updated its guidance on the Azure Migrate process and its agentless migration of VMware workloads over to Azure.

Historically, Microsoft documentation has instructed admins to install VMware VDDK on the Azure Migrate appliance. Now though, Microsoft has added a disclaimer or warning to their official guidance that Broadcom may restrict access to the VDDK.

So, basically, they are saying if you can’t get your hands on the VDDK, then you need to use the agent-based migration instead of the agentless migration method. So, this helps to put the nail in the coffin on the question of whether or not this is a real development or not. You can read the full Microsoft guidance here: Set up an Azure Migrate appliance for server assessment in a VMware environment .

Red Hat has also published a support article on August 27, 2026, which you can find here: Unable to download VMware VDDK images for Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV) . So, this is also an issue for organizations migrating VMware workloads into OpenShift Virtualization. The KB says that customers may receive a “not found” or “access denied” error.

Since the software is proprietary to Broadcom, Red Hat is saying they can’t host or redistribute the package itself. So, they are simply asking customers to contact Broadcom support to request access.

Because VDDK is proprietary Broadcom software, Red Hat says it cannot host or redistribute the package itself. Red Hat looks to also be investigating long term alternatives to remove or work around the dependency on the VDDK.

Red Hat Engineering is also investigating longer-term alternatives to remove or work around the dependency. They make mention of using something like a storage copy offload, but this will depend on the underlying storage vendor and its capabilities.

So, yet another environment that is affected by this is Nutanix. Nutanix customers have now hit this snag as well. A Nutanix community user has noted that they were preparing a migration from ESXi to AHV with the Nutanix Move utility but they found that the VDDK link gave them a 404, even after they logged into their Broadcom account.

Read my blog on the Nutanix Move utility here: Nutanix Move: Migrate from VMware ESXi Free Download .

items.title: La governance dell'acqua tra cultura e democrazia
items.summary: AnsaIncontra verso Forum Euromediterraneo Acqua con Pichetto Fratin, Spena e Giordani
items.content:
L'acqua è una risorsa naturale, ma anche un tema geopolitico, sociale, economico e culturale. Nel Mediterraneo, uno dei territori più esposti agli effetti della crisi climatica, la sua gestione rappresenta una sfida strategica. A poche settimane dal primo Forum Euromediterraneo dell'Acqua, che si terrà a Roma dal 29 settembre al 2 ottobre 2026, un ANSA Incontra propone una riflessione sul rapporto tra governance, innovazione, cultura e democrazia.

Durante l'appuntamento, che sarà trasmesso in streaming martedì 8 settembre alle ore 12 su Ansa.it e sui canali social dell'agenzia, dialogheranno con i giornalisti dell'ANSA Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, ministro dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica, Simonetta Giordani, segretaria Generale Associazione Civita, Maria Spena, presidente Comitato One Water - Forum Euromediterraneo dell'Acqua 2026.

items.title: Erutta un vulcano in Indonesia, fermo l'aeroporto di Giacarta
items.summary: 'Da sabato voli rinviati o cancellati per 340.000 passeggeri'
items.content:
Una enorme fiammata che illumina la notte, poi ceneri e lapilli che riempiono l'aria e una colonna di fumo grigio che si alza gigantesca verso il cielo.

Tra venerdì e sabato, il vulcano Anak Krakatau è tornato a eruttare costringendo per motivi di sicurezza a fermare momentaneamente decolli e atterraggi in otto aeroporti dell'Indonesia: compreso quello di Soekarno-Hatta, che serve la capitale Giacarta. I media internazionali parlano di rinvii e cancellazioni di quasi 3.000 voli per "centinaia di migliaia" di passeggeri: oltre 340.000 da sabato, afferma il governo indonesiano.

Inizialmente, le autorità prevedevano di riaprire lo scalo di Giacarta alle 18 di lunedì, ma successivamente hanno rimandato per sicurezza di almeno sei ore, come minimo fino allo scoccare della mezzanotte tra lunedì e martedì, sottolinea la Bbc, che intanto riferisce di lunghe code di passeggeri nel principale aeroporto della capitale indonesiana. "La direzione del vento è molto variabile" e le autorità "vogliono avere la certezza assoluta che la cenere vulcanica si allontani dalle aree aeroportuali", ha detto il ministro dei Trasporti indonesiano Dudy Purwagandhi.

Da Giacarta il vulcano Anak Krakatau dista appena 150 chilometri . E oggi nell'aria c'era ancora cenere vulcanica, mentre l'agenzia geologica indonesiana definiva "alta" la possibilità di altre eruzioni. L'agenzia di stampa locale Antara riporta che alle scuole della zona è stato ordinato di svolgere per ora le lezioni da remoto. E secondo la France Presse, il governo indonesiano ha detto di aver predisposto "sei aeroporti alternativi - tra cui quelli di Giava Orientale, Giava Centrale e Yogyakarta - come opzioni per i voli originariamente diretti a Giacarta", mentre "i gestori aeroportuali metteranno a disposizione servizi di autobus gratuiti per i passeggeri che desiderano partire da altri aeroporti".

L'Anak Krakatau è emerso dalle acque circa un secolo fa e il suo nome significa "figlio di Krakatoa": un vulcano che si trovava proprio in questa zona tra Giava e Sumatra e che nel 1883 fu in gran parte distrutto da una serie di violente eruzioni che uccisero 36.000 persone.

Alla fine del 2018, una potente eruzione dell'Anak Krakatau provocò invece uno tsunami che uccise più di 400 persone. Con i suoi 127 vulcani attivi, l'Indonesia si trova nel pieno della cosiddetta "Cintura di Fuoco": una zona altamente sismica a forma di arco che attraversa il mondo per decine di chilometri snodandosi dalle zone orientali dell'Asia e dell'Oceania fino a quelle occidentali delle Americhe.

items.title: Elezioni in Sassonia-Anhalt, Merz scioccato. 'Scossi nelle fondamenta ma non mi arrendo'
items.summary: Il giorno buio del cancelliere che prova a rassicurare. L'Afd ne chiede le dimissioni
items.content:
La Cdu di Adenauer "scossa nelle fondamenta". Il cancelliere "scioccato". Il giorno dopo il voto della Sassonia-Anhalt, che ha visto l'ultradestra di Ulrich Siegmund sfondare con il 43,8%, la retorica a Berlino si carica di una tensione drammatica atipica per un paese del nordeuropa.

Ma Friedrich Merz non è disposto a pagare il conto della svolta storica avvenuta a Magdeburgo, dove il suo partito è crollato al 17,2%. "Arrendermi non è un'opzione" , ha risposto a chi in conferenza stampa gli ha chiesto quando ne avrà viste abbastanza, da poter pensare alle dimissioni.

Dal campo opposto, la leader di Afd Alice Weidel lo ha attaccato frontalmente , chiedendo che si faccia da parte: "La Cdu ha subito una debacle, un risultato che si riflette a livello federale, le persone hanno perso la fiducia. Nessun cancelliere prima era stato così impopolare come Friedrich Merz, che è diventato un grande peso per lo sviluppo in Germania". Poi ha ripetuto la sua analisi della situazione: "La Germania è de facto in bancarotta. Non vi dicono i dati ma è fallita. Come la Francia del resto". "Quando saremo al governo - ha scandito tornando sul mantra del partito - chiuderemo le frontiere, perché la politica dei confini aperti non è più finanziabile".

I dati emersi dalle urne portano alla conclusione che il governo nel piccolo Land dell'Est conquistato da Siegmund debba essere governato da Alternativa, che metterà su un esecutivo per la prima volta. E per la Bild il cancelliere inizierebbe ad adeguarsi all'idea che sia meglio lasciare che a governare siano proprio loro - la mano tesa di Sahra Wagneknecht del Bsw (entrato nel parlamentino) lo consentirebbe - "lasciando che commettano i loro errori". Si rovineranno da soli, è il senso del ragionamento. Anche perché il programma radicale col quale hanno trionfato è in gran parte non realizzabile, e riempirà la regione di debiti, nella lettura di molti politici sul territorio. È stato dunque Sven Schulze, il governatore democristiano uscente sconfitto ad affermare: "Non abbiamo il mandato per governare. Spetta a Afd".

Merz però ha tenuto a rassicurare anche chi osserva il Paese dall'esterno. "Il governo farà in modo che la Costituzione si imponga. Lo dico anche per i nostri partner europei e internazionali. Sappiamo che per la nostra storia la Germania ha una responsabilità particolare. Manterremo l'ordine politico, e resteremo ancorati all'Europa".

L'analisi fatta a porte chiuse nella Cdu, trapelata dalla Bild, ha messo in chiaro che il "sistema partitico sta subendo uno sconvolgimento" e che "questo scuote il nostro partito nelle fondamenta", per il cancelliere. Tutti i grandi partiti popolari rischiano il nanismo , dopo l'Spd ora anche l'Unione dei conservatori. Ma quali sono le risposte di Friedrich Merz in questa tragica situazione? In realtà si stenta a trovarle. Merz appare senza strategie. E in effetti il discorso col quale ha spiegato di non voler mollare non ha convinto nessuno. I consensi personali alla deriva? "Cerco le ragioni anche dentro di me", ha risposto.

La svolta del Land che ha voltato le spalle al suo partito? Bisogna cambiare narrativa, parlare meglio il linguaggio delle emozioni, è la proposta del Bundeskanzler, che a questo punto intende "prendere molto sul serio le paure, le preoccupazioni dei concittadini" e raggiungere i tedeschi con "dedizione ed empatia". Due parole nuove nel suo lessico politico.

Una ricetta che ha lasciato insoddisfatti i principali analisti della capitale, a partire dalla potentissima Bild, che continua ad attaccarlo. E potrebbero iniziare a prendere le distanze anche gli alleati socialdemocratici, i quali vogliono ritrattare le riforme e stando alla Sz credono sempre meno che Merz sia la guida giusta. Queste invece restano "necessarie" e "sono la chance per il futuro dei nostri figli e dei nostri nipoti" per il cancelliere che da oggi vuole essere più empatico.

items.title: Regno Unito, caos a Portsmouth: anti-migranti incappucciati assediano il porto
items.summary: In centinaia come a Dover, scontri con la polizia. Il governo Burnham: 'Teppisti'
items.content:
L'onda dell'estrema destra anti-migranti si estende nel Regno Unito con una nuova protesta segnata da episodi di violenza . Alcuni agenti sono rimasti feriti, non in modo grave, e diversi veicoli della polizia sono stati danneggiati domenica sera quando circa 500 persone hanno tentato di marciare a Portsmouth, nella contea dell'Hampshire , e hanno creato disagi al traffico stradale e agli imbarchi per i traghetti, dopo aver saputo dello sbarco nel porto inglese affacciato sulla Manica di un gruppo di 140 migranti.

La polizia locale e la guardia di frontiera sono intervenute in assetto anti-sommossa per impedire ai gruppi di raggiungere l'area dove erano trattenuti i migranti: molti dei manifestanti indossavano il cappuccio e si erano coperti il volto per evitare di essere riconosciuti dalle forze dell'ordine. I migranti sono stati poi trasferiti in un centro di Dover e alcuni dei militanti dell'ultradestra hanno seguito il convoglio di veicoli della Border Force per filmare video e postarli sui social media.

Quanto accaduto segue la 'marcia' analoga svoltasi sabato scorso proprio a Dover , sede di un importante centro di prima accoglienza, dove il porto è stato bloccato per un paio d'ore da alcune centinaia di individui vestiti di nero e col volto mascherato da passamontagna. Una sorta di 'uniforme', diventata un tratto distintivo di queste azioni - anche se a Portsmouth un numero inferiore di persone la indossava - scandite da slogan contro le "small boat", le piccole imbarcazioni che trasportano migranti illegali dalla Francia alle coste inglesi attraverso il Canale.

Entrambe le manifestazioni sono state animate e organizzate da Daniel Thomas, alias Danny Tommo, già autista e guardaspalle di Tommy Robinson, animatore di gruppi dell'ultradestra inglese, già condannato per reati comuni, oltre che processato per razzismo e istigazione a violenze di piazza e all'odio contro migranti e musulmani, noto pure per le simpatie che da qualche tempo raccoglie da parte di esponenti del governo israeliano di Benyamin Netanyahu.

I due negli ultimi mesi hanno lavorato alla creazione della cosiddetta Patriot Platform, che riunisce gruppi locali di estrema destra, autodefinitisi "patrioti" sulla base dell'ostilità verso l'immigrazione, provenienti soprattutto dal sud dell'Inghilterra ma anche dal nord-ovest. Si tratta di "teppismo" secondo il governo laburista di Andy Burnham, che ha condannato con forza le manifestazioni degenerate in scontri con la polizia pur assicurando la tutela di "ogni protesta pacifica".

Mentre il leader del trumpiano Reform Uk, Nigel Farage, noto per le sue posizioni anti-immigrazione, in un video su X ha dichiarato che il Paese è sull'orlo di "gravi disordini civili" e ha criticato il governo, ma ha anche condannato chi protesta col volto coperto e in un'uniforme da paramilitare, ricordando che ogni manifestazione deve rispettare la legge.

Uno dei suoi collaboratori più stretti, Zia Yusuf, ha parlato con Tommo, dopo che quest'ultimo si era intromesso all'improvviso in un'intervista davanti alle telecamere. L'organizzatore delle proteste ha detto che Farage non deve usare parole offensive contro i militanti di ultradestra e di voler creare un "blocco elettorale" in cerca del "partito giusto per cui votare".

items.title: Nuovi raid israeliani in Libano, sterminata una famiglia
items.summary: Morti anche 2 neonati. L'Idf accusa Hezbollah. Nel sud spuntano strade israeliane per restare
items.content:
L'escalation militare a lungo annunciata da Israele contro le roccaforti civili e militari di Hezbollah, il partito di resistenza armata sostenuto dall'Iran, mostra oggi la sua punta più sanguinosa e visibile nel contesto formale di un "cessate il fuoco" sempre più evanescente: circa 30 persone uccise in 72 ore nel sud del Libano, tra cui neonati, soccorritori e combattenti del partito di Dio .

Sul terreno compaiono intanto n uove strade e terrapieni militari israeliani , un segnale, secondo analisti libanesi, della volontà dello Stato ebraico di restare a lungo come forza occupante nel sud del Libano.

Israele giustifica l'inasprimento dei raid come risposta ad attacchi di Hezbollah: contro soldati israeliani che si trovano però in pieno territorio libanese e che con la loro stessa azione violano il cessate il fuoco.

L'escalation sta maturando a poche settimane dagli attesi nuovi negoziati di Roma, mediati da Washington tra Beirut e Israele, e nel contesto di una tensione regionale crescente tra fronte americano e iraniano che si estende da Hormuz a Bab al-Mandab. In questo quadro, un'intera famiglia è stata sterminata all'alba a Kfar Remman, nel distretto di Nabatiye, cuore degli scontri per il controllo delle alture strategiche nella profondità del sud del Libano.

Tra le otto vittime della famiglia Farhat, due neonati e due donne. Hezbollah ammette che tra gli uccisi vi sono anche due suoi membri. Nello stesso raid perdono la vita due soccorritori, per un bilancio di 10 uccisi. Nei bombardamenti da venerdì a oggi risultano complessivamente 27 uccisi e decine di feriti.

Secondo il ministero della sanità di Beirut, dall'inizio del nuovo round di guerra, il 2 marzo scorso, Israele ha ucciso 4.381 persone in Libano e ne ha ferite 12.402 . Dal canto suo Israele afferma che il raid su Kfar Remman ha colpito un'infrastruttura di Hezbollah "in risposta al lancio di droni" contro le sue forze nel sud del Libano.

Come ulteriore segnale del deterioramento della situazione, l'esercito israeliano ha allertato gli abitanti della Galilea settentrionale di una serie di attacchi imminenti in territorio libanese le cui esplosioni potrebbero essere udite anche in territorio israeliano. In questo quadro, la società civile libanese è tornata a mobilitarsi su due fronti opposti: da un lato, per chiedere il dispiegamento dell'esercito regolare a Nabatiye e il ritiro e disarmo di Hezbollah "per salvare Nabatiye"; dall'altro, tramite i sindaci delle località meridionali occupate, storicamente identificate con la resistenza del partito di Dio, che protestano contro il governo di Beirut, accusato di non fare abbastanza per impedire a Israele di distruggere oltre 60 località del sud del Libano, ostacolandone così il ritorno di lungo periodo.
